Glowno Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Głowno, Poland

Demolished. Głowno, a private noble town granted rights in 1427, saw Jewish settlement begin in 1730 when the town's owner actively recruited Jewish craftsmen and traders to revive the local economy; by 1827, 77% (784) of residents were Jewish, still 59% (1,430) by 1921. A May 1940 ghetto held over 7,000 people, including Jews relocated from Konstantynów Łódzki, Brzeziny, Zgierz, and Aleksandrów Łódzki; in March 1941 residents were transported to the Warsaw Ghetto and then Treblinka. This cemetery, likely founded in the mid-18th century, had its tombstones used to harden roads during WWII; postwar authorities approved a factory on the site, and a 1975 artificial lake (Mrożyczka) was created nearby. Recovered tombstone fragments, the oldest dated 1812, are preserved at the Regional Museum in Głowno.
